Subject: Performance SLO qualification — streaming & cost levers

Thanks for the time today, Jessica — good conversation. Quick recap + proposed next steps from our side. Please flag anything I missed.

Call recap (tl;dr):
- Primary SLO: interactive chat experience. p95 first-token latency target: <= 200ms (goal 150ms) for short prompts (~32 tokens).
- Sustained throughput: expected peak concurrency 150–300 concurrent users, average 80–120 concurrent.
- Streaming required: yes — token-level streaming to the client with low initial latency is critical.
- Quality: some outputs are quality-sensitive (medical triage language) — fallback to higher-quality model variant when needed.

Open questions we flagged on the call:
1) Typical prompt size distribution and average generated token length (you mentioned 20–50 tokens generated).
2) Traffic shape (spiky times, global regions) — any region-specific peaks?
3) Whether certain flows can accept slightly higher tail latency in exchange for cost savings.

Initial cost/performance levers (high-level):
- Continuous batching: reduces per-token cost by aggregating requests, configurable batch windows (tradeoff: wider windows reduce cost but can increase tail latency).
- Prefix/KV caching: for repeated prompts or assistant-system-context reuse — can dramatically reduce compute for warm sessions.
- Quantization profiles: 8-bit/4-bit options. 4-bit QC lowers GPU memory and unit cost but sometimes impacts quality; we recommend 4-bit for lower-critical flows and 8-bit for sensitive flows.
- Model variants: smaller/quantized variants for baseline, larger unquantized model for quality-critical requests with automatic fallback policies.

Proposed next steps:
- Rishi/Dylan: run a 1-hour benchmark on a small sample trace you provide (we'll use both streaming and non-streaming modes).
- Jessica: share 1–2 representative request traces + target traffic curve (CSV or replay script).
- Marissa: follow up with preliminary cost estimate and reserved capacity options.

I'm attaching a short SLO template + cost-levers workbook (orchid-performance-slo.pdf, orchid-cost-levers.xlsx).

Thanks — available for a 30m deep-dive Wed or Thu if helpful.

Best,

Thanks Rishi — this is super helpful. A few clarifications from our side:‎
- Streaming requirement: yes, initial token latency is the most important metric for our UI. We need the first token <200ms 95% of the time in the US region. Subsequent tokens can stream at ~20–30ms per chunk.
- Concurrency: Peak users map to ~250 concurrent active chats during business hours (mostly US East/West). Background batch jobs (non-streaming) account for ~50 RPS off-peak.
- Payloads: average prompt size ~180 characters (~35 tokens), generated length averages 30–40 tokens.

2) For continuous batching, what batch window would you recommend to keep p95 first-token under 200ms at 250 concurrent?

On Mon, Mar 22, 2027 at 9:15 AM Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com> wrote:
> Call recap (tl;dr):
> - Primary SLO: interactive chat experience. p95 first-token latency target: <= 200ms (goal 150ms) for short prompts (~32 tokens).
> - Sustained throughput: expected peak concurrency 150–300 concurrent users, average 80–120 concurrent.
> - Streaming required: yes — token-level streaming to the client with low initial latency is critical.

Answers to your questions: 
1) 4-bit quantization impact: cold-start latency is typically similar (model load happens at pod spin-up) but per-token execution is faster and uses less memory. For streaming jitter, 4-bit runs can be slightly less consistent on very short chunk intervals because of packing/bit-unpack overhead on some kernels — in our benchmarks we see ~5–15ms additional variance on sub-20ms chunk intervals. Recommendation: use 4-bit for baseline flows; reserve 8-bit (or FP16) model variants for the quality-sensitive triage flows.

2) Continuous batching and batch window: to keep p95 first-token under 200ms at ~250 concurrent, we recommend a conservative batch window of 5–10ms with a max-batch-size tuned to your expected concurrency. Continuous batching with a 5ms window + prefix caching for warm sessions should meet your 150–200ms target in US regions on our dedicated instance types. We'll validate during the replay benchmark.

Additional notes: 
- Prefix/KV caching: supported with per-tenant namespaces. We can scope cache keys to tenant IDs so you get caching benefits without cross-tenant leakage.
- Streaming chunk size: aim for 8–16 token chunking for steady token throughput (~20–30ms per chunk on our infra).
- Autoscaling and warm pools: for sudden spikes we recommend a small warm pool to avoid pod spin-up affecting your p95. This is part of a Dedicated/Reserved config (Marissa can share numbers).

Next steps (concrete):
- Rishi/Dylan: run replay benchmark Wed 3/24 10am PT using the traces you share. We'll test 3 configs: (A) 4-bit quantized baseline with 5ms batch window + caching, (B) 8-bit / FP16 with 5ms window, (C) hybrid: 4-bit baseline + automatic fallback to 8-bit for flagged prompts.
- Jessica: share trace + golden prompts + a short priority map for quality-sensitive flows.
- Marissa: share preliminary pricing estimate and reserved capacity options for a 6-month pilot.

Attachments: I re-attached the SLO summary and cost workbook.

I'll kick off the benchmark as soon as we have the traces.

Thanks,
Rishi
